title: Mahajanaka's swim
hook: a shipwrecked prince swims on with no shore in sight
tomorrow: can hard work actually feel good?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lute string: too tight snaps, too loose thuds. Energy for good is tuned. Today, effort when you can't see where it ends.

A long rehab, a job hunt, a skill that isn't clicking yet: some efforts have no finish line you can see. You send the next application without knowing if anyone reads it. In the Jataka, Prince Mahajanaka is sailing out to make his fortune when the ship breaks apart in open sea. The others panic. He eats a full meal, rubs his body with oil, climbs the mast, leaps as far clear of the wreck as he can, and starts swimming. Tradition says he swims for seven days. No shore in sight.
screen: `NO FINISH LINE IN SIGHT.` → `THE SHIP BREAKS APART.` → `HE STARTS SWIMMING.`

segments.voice: Then a sea goddess, Manimekhala, notices him. In the story she asks the obvious question: why work so hard out here, where no shore can be seen? His answer is the lesson. Someone who keeps striving, he says, can't be blamed; even if he goes down, he goes down having done what was his to do. She tells him his effort is useless in an ocean this size. He holds his ground. And moved by it, she lifts him up and carries him to land. Notice the order. He doesn't swim because he can see the shore. He swims, and then help arrives. Tradition remembers this tale as the Bodhisatta perfecting effort. It sounds like tough-guy advice, but look at what he did first: he ate, he oiled his skin against the sea, he chose his moment to jump. Swim anyway isn't thrash anyway. The Dhammapada has a line for him. In Max Müller's words: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm."
screen: `WHY SWIM WHERE NO SHORE SHOWS?` · `ONE WHO STRIVES ISN'T BLAMED.` · `HE ATE, OILED, CHOSE HIS JUMP.` · `MAKE YOURSELF AN ISLAND.` · then, large: `SWIM ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you've been tempted to drop because you can't see the end of it. Name what's most likely to stop you this week, and decide your next small stroke for when it does. Hold that plan in mind while the sit runs.
Mahajanaka's swim: effort that keeps going without seeing the shore, after doing the sensible things first.
Something to keep: swim anyway, because the goddess came on the seventh day, not the first. Talk tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1559 COUNTS.` → `THE TEN PERFECTIONS · DAY 14 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: CAN HARD WORK ACTUALLY FEEL GOOD?`

howItsDone: The Mahajanaka Jataka is one of the last ten Jataka tales, which tradition ties to the ten perfections; it is retold in sermons and on temple walls in Theravada countries as the tale of effort.
